items.question: What do you think Veo’s ability to model liquids reveals about how AI learns physical behavior?
items.object: Veo’s ability to model physical behavior
items.answer: I mean, fluid dynamics, Navier-Stokes equations, these are traditionally thought of as very, very difficult, intractable problems to do on classical systems. They take enormous amounts of compute. Weather prediction systems, these kinds of things, all involve fluid dynamics calculations. But again, if you look at something like Veo, our video generation model, it can model liquids quite well, surprisingly well, and materials, specular lighting. I love the ones where people have generated videos where there's clear liquids going through hydraulic presses and then being squeezed out. I used to write physics engines and graphics engines in my early days in gaming. And I know it's just so painstakingly hard to build programs that can do that. And yet somehow these systems are reverse engineering from just watching YouTube videos. So presumably what's happening is it's extracting some underlying structure around how these materials behave. So perhaps there is some kind of lower-dimensional manifold that can be learned if we actually fully understood what's going on under the hood. That's maybe true of most of reality.

items.question: Why do you think natural systems shaped by evolution can be efficiently modeled by classical learning algorithms?
items.object: The conjecture that natural systems shaped by evolution can be efficiently modeled by classical learning algorithms
items.answer: If you take a step back and you look at all the work that we've done, especially with the Alpha projects, so I'm thinking AlphaGo, of course, AlphaFold, what they really are is we're building models of very combinatorially high-dimensional spaces that, if you tried to brute force a solution, find the best move in Go, or find the exact shape of a protein, and if you enumerated all the possibilities, there wouldn't be enough time in the time of the universe. So you have to do something much smarter. And what we did in both cases was build models of those environments, and that guided the search in a smart way, and that makes it tractable. So if you think about protein folding, which is obviously a natural system, why should that be possible? How does physics do that? Proteins fold in milliseconds in our bodies. So somehow physics solves this problem that we've now also solved computationally. And I think the reason that's possible is that in nature, natural systems have structure because they were subject to evolutionary processes that shape them. And if that's true, then you can maybe learn what that structure is. So this perspective, I think, is a really interesting one. You've hinted at it, which is, crudely stated, anything that can be evolved can be efficiently modeled. I think there's some truth to that.

items.question: Why do you think natural structures shaped over time could be efficiently learned by neural networks?
items.object: The learnability of natural structures through “survival of the stablest”
items.answer: I sometimes call it survival of the stablest or something like that, because of course there's evolution for living things, but there's also, if you think about geological time, the shape of mountains that's been shaped by weathering processes over thousands of years. But then you can even take it cosmological: the orbits of planets, the shapes of asteroids. These have all survived processes that have acted on them many, many times. So if that's true, then there should be some sort of pattern that you can kind of reverse learn, and a kind of manifold, really, that helps you search to the right solution, to the right shape, and actually allow you to predict things about it in an efficient way, because it's not a random pattern. So it may not be possible for man-made things or abstract things like factorizing large numbers, because unless there's patterns in the number space, which there might be, but if there's not and it's uniform, then there's no pattern to learn, there's no model to learn that will help you search. So you have to do brute force. So in that case, maybe you need a quantum computer, something like this. But most things in nature that we're interested in are not like that. They have structure that evolved for a reason and survived over time. And if that's true, I think that's potentially learnable by a neural network.

items.question: How far do you think the approach used in AlphaGo and AlphaFold—learning a system's dynamics to make finding solutions efficient—can take classical computers?
items.object: The learned-model paradigm used in AlphaGo and AlphaFold and the capabilities of classical computers
items.answer: I think that there are actually a huge class of problems that could be couched in this way, the way we did AlphaGo and the way we did AlphaFold, where you model the dynamics of the system, the properties of that system, the environment that you're trying to understand, and then that makes the search for the solution or the prediction of the next step efficient, basically polynomial time, so tractable by a classical system, which a neural network is. It runs on normal computers, classical computers, Turing machines in effect. And I think it's one of the most interesting questions there is: how far can that paradigm go? I think we've proven, and the AI community in general, that classical systems, Turing machines, can go a lot further than we previously thought. They can do things like model the structures of proteins and play Go to better than world champion level. A lot of people would have thought maybe 10 or 20 years ago that was decades away, or maybe you would need some sort of quantum machines, quantum systems, to be able to do things like protein folding. And so I think we haven't really even scratched the surface yet of what classical systems could do.

items.question: Why do you think problems with enormous numbers of possible configurations can still be tractable for neural networks?
items.object: Using neural networks to model seemingly intractable problems
items.answer: There's some structure, some landscape in the energy landscape or whatever it is, that you can follow, some gradient you can follow. And of course what neural networks are very good at is following gradients. And so if there's one to follow and an objective, and you can specify the objective function correctly, you don't have to deal with all that complexity, which I think is how we maybe naively thought about it for decades. Those problems, if you just enumerate all the possibilities, look totally intractable. And there are many, many problems like that. You think, well, it's 10 to the 300 possible protein structures, it's 10 to the 70 possible Go positions. All of these are way more than atoms in the universe, so how could one possibly find the right solution or predict the next step? But it turns out that it is possible. And of course reality, nature, does do it, right? Proteins do fold. That gives you confidence that there must be, if we understood how physics was doing that and could mimic that process, model that process, it should be possible on our classical systems. That's basically what the conjecture is about.

You've got to be able to create content whichever direction the player goes in, and you want it to be compelling no matter what the player chooses. It was always quite difficult to build things like cellular automata, those kinds of classical systems which created some emergent behavior. But they were always a little bit fragile, a little bit limited. Now we're maybe on the cusp, in the next five or ten years, of having AI systems that can truly create around your imagination, can dynamically change the story and tell the narrative around it, and make it dramatic no matter what you end up choosing. items.question: How do you think search processes can help AI systems discover something genuinely new?
items.object: Search processes for discovery and creativity in AI systems
items.answer: If you think about breaking down the systems we've built to their really fundamental core, you've got the model of the underlying dynamics of the system. If you want to discover something new, something novel that hasn't been seen before, then you need some kind of search process on top to take you to a novel region of the search space. You can do that in a number of ways. Evolutionary computing is one. With AlphaGo we just use Monte Carlo tree search, and that's what found move 37, the new kind of never-seen-before strategy in Go. That's how you can go beyond potentially what is already known. The model can model everything that you currently know about, all the data that you currently have, but then how do you go beyond that? That starts to speak about the ideas of creativity: how can these systems create something new, discover something new? This is super relevant for scientific discovery or pushing medicine forward, which we want to do with these systems. You can actually bolt on some fairly simple search systems on top of these models and get you into a new region of space. Of course, you also have to make sure that you're not searching that space totally randomly. It would be too big. So you have to have some objective function that you're trying to optimize and hill-climb towards, and that guides that search. But there's some mechanisms of evolution that are interesting, maybe in the space of programs. The space of programs is an extremely important space because you can probably generalize to everything.

items.question: How do you envision building Virtual Cell, your project to simulate an entire cell?
items.object: Virtual Cell, a project to simulate an entire cell
items.answer: Virtual Cell, which is what I call the project of modeling a cell, I've had this idea for maybe more like 25 years. I used to talk with Paul Nurse, who is a bit of a mentor of mine in biology. He runs the Crick Institute and won the Nobel Prize in 2001. We've been talking about it since before the '90s, and I come back to it every five years: what would you need to model the full internals of a cell so that you could do experiments on the virtual cell, and those experiments and predictions would be useful to save you a lot of time in the wet lab? That would be the dream. Maybe you could 100x speed up experiments by doing most of it in silico, the search in silico, and then do the validation step in the wet lab. That's the dream. I was trying to build these components, AlphaFold being one, that would allow you eventually to model the full interactions, a full simulation of a cell. I'd probably start with a yeast cell, partly because that's what Paul Nurse studied. A yeast cell is a full organism that's a single cell, so it's the simplest single-cell organism. It's not just a cell, it's a full organism, and yeast is very well understood, so that would be a good candidate for a full simulated model. AlphaFold is the solution to the static picture of what a protein's 3D structure looks like. But in biology, all the interesting things happen with the dynamics, the interactions, and that's what AlphaFold 3 is the first step towards, modeling those interactions. First pairwise, proteins with proteins, proteins with RNA and DNA, but then the next step would be modeling maybe a whole pathway, maybe the pathway that's involved in cancer, and then eventually you might be able to model a whole cell.

items.question: What standard would you use to decide whether an AI system has achieved artificial general intelligence?

items.answer: Mine's quite a high bar and always has been: can we match the cognitive functions that the brain has? We know our brains are pretty much general Turing machines, approximately. We've created incredible modern civilization with our minds, so that speaks to how general the brain is. For us to know we have a true AGI, we'd have to make sure that it has all those capabilities. It isn't a kind of jagged intelligence, where some things it's really good at, like today's systems, but other things it's really flawed at. items.question: How do you assess whether further AI progress will come from scaling existing methods or from new research breakthroughs?

items.answer: We certainly feel there's a lot more room just in the scaling. All steps: pre-training, post-training, and inference time. There are three scalings happening concurrently. Again, it's about how innovative you can be. We pride ourselves on having the broadest and deepest research bench. We have amazing researchers and people like Noam Shazeer, who came up with Transformers, and David Silver, who led the AlphaGo project. That research base means that if some new breakthrough is required, like AlphaGo or Transformers, I would back us to be the place that does that. It's harder to invent things than to fast-follow. We don't know; I'd say it's kind of 50/50 whether new things are needed or whether scaling existing stuff is going to be enough. items.object: Cautious optimism as an approach to AI's benefits and risks

We want the outcome, the benefits and amazing things AI can bring. items.question: How do you compare the risks of humans misusing AI with the risks of losing control over increasingly autonomous AI systems?
items.object: Human misuse of AI versus loss of control over autonomous AI
items.answer: I think they operate over different timescales and they're equally important to address. There's the common, garden-variety bad actors using new technology, in this case general-purpose technology, and repurposing it for harmful ends. That's a huge risk. I think that has a lot of complications because generally I'm in huge favor of open science and open source. In fact, we did it with all our science projects like AlphaFold for the benefit of the scientific community. But how does one restrict bad actors' access to these powerful systems, whether they're individuals or rogue states, and enable access at the same time to good actors to maximally build on top of them? It's a pretty tricky problem. I've not heard a clear solution. So there's the bad actor use-case problem, and then as the systems become more agentic and closer to AGI and more autonomous, how do we ensure the guardrails stick to what we want them to do and keep them under our control? I tend to maybe worry more about the humans, the bad actors.

items.question: How do you think building AI can help us understand what, if anything, makes the human mind special?
items.object: Building AI to understand what makes the human mind special
items.answer: I think that's what I've always imagined when I was a kid and starting on this journey. I was fascinated by things like consciousness, did a neuroscience PhD to look at how the brain works, especially imagination and memory. I focused on the hippocampus. It's going to be interesting. I always thought the best way, of course, one can philosophize about it and have thought experiments, and maybe even do actual experiments like you do in neuroscience on real brains, but in the end I always imagined that building an AI, a kind of intelligent artifact, and comparing that to the human mind and seeing what the differences were would be the best way to uncover what's special about the human mind, if indeed there's anything special. I suspect there probably is, but it's going to be hard to define. This journey we're on will help us understand and define that. There may be a difference between carbon-based substrates, what we are, and silicon ones when they process information. One of the best definitions I like of consciousness is “it's the information feels when we process it.” It could be an interesting intuitive one, and this scientific journey we're on will help uncover that mystery.

items.question: How do you think about whether consciousness can be modeled by a classical computer?
items.object: Modeling consciousness with classical computers
items.answer: Well, Penrose is an amazing thinker, one of the greatest of the modern era, and we've had a lot of discussions about this. Of course, we cordially disagree. He collaborated with a lot of good neuroscientists to see if he could find mechanisms for quantum mechanics behavior in the brain. To my knowledge, they haven't found anything convincing yet. My bet is that it's mostly just classical computing that's going on in the brain, which suggests that all the phenomena are modelable or mimickable by a classical computer. But we'll see. There may be this final mysterious thing of the feeling of consciousness, the qualia, these kinds of things that philosophers debate, where it's unique to the substrate. We may even come towards understanding that if we do things like Neuralink and have neural interfaces to AI systems, which I think we probably will eventually, maybe to keep up with AI systems. items.question: How do you think models of different parts of the world could contribute to an AGI system?

items.answer: Well, I think one of the obvious unifying factors is, well, of course it all has to obey the laws of physics, at least most of it, maybe apart from consciousness. That's up for debate, maybe that's a different thing. And those models will get better and more complex. Could you build kind of submodels of the world that would be useful for building a general world model that then could be plugged into an AGI system? I think for sure. items.question: How do you think viewing the universe as a computational system could help explain emergence?
items.object: The universe as a computational system and its implications for emergence
items.answer: If you think of physics or reality as a kind of computational universe and the universe as kind of computing itself, then you can imagine that there could be subroutines or different sets of algorithms that the universe is running in different domains. And maybe some of those algorithms require different mathematics to explain them, right? So maybe there is the mathematics of cells. Maybe there's the mathematics of consciousness. And maybe those are not reducible in a simple way to what we call physics, which maybe is some kind of base layer. There are other layers on top that may have different laws, if you will. In the same way you might program a program that works at a higher level than the actual transistor gate level. So I think this idea of the universe having different kinds of computation that it's running, almost like different pieces of code, is a really interesting one, and one that could be potentially useful in explaining what we call emergence. It's a bit like the idea, for example, of a black hole encoding information on its surface, yet somehow it's also inside. We don't quite understand that, and that's maybe because it's computing in a different way than what we have currently figured out.
